sentences.text: Protoalligator was an extinct crocodilian that lived in China during the Paleocene epoch.
The only known specimen, catalogued as IVPP V4058, dates to the middle Paleocene, specifically between 66 and 61.66 million years ago.
This single fossil includes the front part of a mostly preserved right skull and the front section of the lower jaw, retaining some teeth in their sockets.
The proportions of the remains suggest the animal possessed a relatively short snout, featuring an anterior process on the premaxilla that extended over the external naris.
Its eleventh and twelfth lower teeth were the largest in the posterior mouth area, a trait distinguishing it from modern alligators.
Unlike Asiatosuchus nanlingensis and many alligatoroids, the tip of the fourth lower tooth in Protoalligator is covered by a fossa located between the maxilla and premaxilla.
The remains of Protoalligator huiningensis were first discovered in 1966 in Huaining County, Anhui Province, China.
These fossils were found in the Wanghudun Formation of China.
Protoalligator was first described as a species of Eoalligator by Yang Zhongjian in 1982.
The name Protoalligator was coined in 2016 by Y. Wang, C. Sullivan, and J. Liu specifically for E. huiningensis after E. chunyii was synonymized with Asiatosuchus nanlingensis.
Protoalligator had an overbite, as all lower jaw teeth except the enlarged fourth one occluded medially to the upper jaw teeth.
A 2016 phylogenetic analysis suggests Protoalligator is a member of Alligatoroidea, indicated by its long surangular process.
The genus Protoalligator was named by Y. Wang, C. Sullivan, and J. Liu in 2016.
The type species of the genus Protoalligator is Protoalligator huiningensis.
Eoalligator huiningensis is a synonym of Protoalligator huiningensis.
Protoalligator was placed in its own genus in 2016 by Wang, Sullivan, and Liu.
It is debated whether Protoalligator belongs to the group Orientalosuchina and whether that group consists of alligatoroids.
It is debated whether Protoalligator belongs to the clade Orientalosuchina, as some studies exclude it from the group.
Subsequent authors have continued to treat Protoalligator and Eoalligator as separate taxa despite their close relationship.
